title: AI Takes the Wheel in Fusion Experiments, Reacting in Milliseconds
summary:
In the quest for fusion energy — the same process that powers the sun — scientists face a daunting challenge: plasma can become unstable within a few thousandths of a second, far too fast for any human to respond. Now, researchers at the Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL) and Princeton University have developed an AI framework called PACMAN that can make those split-second decisions while keeping humans in charge of the overall goals.

PACMAN, which stands for Prediction And Control using MAchiNe learning, was tested on a real fusion device in five separate experiments. The results are published in the journal Nuclear Fusion.

Fusion machines like tokamaks use powerful magnetic fields to confine plasma — an electrically charged gas. For fusion to work, the plasma must remain hot, dense, and stable. But even small disturbances can grow into instabilities that disrupt the reaction within milliseconds.

Traditional computer simulations can take days or months to run, making them useless for real-time control. "For control we need models that make a decision in the moment," said co-lead author Hiro Farre Kaga. "Machine learning models are the only way we have to model the plasma in millisecond times."

PACMAN operates in a repeating control loop that runs about every 20 milliseconds. "A really focused human operator can respond on the order of seconds," said co-lead author Andy Rothstein. "The whole PACMAN framework typically runs in about 20 milliseconds, and it's not running once. It's running again and again and again."

The system works like an assembly line with four stations: it collects live measurements, checks them for errors, uses AI models to predict plasma behavior, and then controllers determine the necessary actions. Finally, it resolves conflicting instructions and applies hardware safety limits before sending commands to the tokamak.

One of the most striking demonstrations was with the tearing mode, an instability that conventional controllers can only detect after it starts. PACMAN's machine learning model predicted it about 200 milliseconds in advance, allowing the plasma to be adjusted to avoid it altogether.

This framework's modular design means scientists can add new models without disrupting the whole system. As fusion research advances, AI like PACMAN could be crucial for making fusion a practical, clean energy source. The future of power might just be in the hands of intelligent machines.
why_it_matters: Fusion reactors could one day produce nearly limitless clean energy, but keeping the plasma stable is a balancing act that happens in milliseconds. If AI can reliably make those split-second decisions, it moves fusion from theory toward real power plants — while also raising important questions about when to trust machines with physical hardware.

background_read: Fusion is the nuclear reaction that powers the Sun; on Earth it would combine light atoms to release energy without producing carbon dioxide, and its fuel can be extracted from water.
To do that, reactors called tokamaks (donut-shaped machines first developed in fusion research programs) create a very hot plasma and surround it with magnetic fields so it never touches the walls.

The Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL, a U.S. Department of Energy national laboratory managed by Princeton University) and Princeton University (a private research university in New Jersey) have spent decades studying this problem.

Because plasma disruptions can appear faster than humans can react, the field has turned to machine learning; PACMAN is one recent example but not the only attempt to give plasma control a faster 'brain.'
Fusion energy is not yet practical — scientists also need to produce more energy than the reactor consumes — but AI controllers like PACMAN aim to solve one of the major obstacles on the way.

perspectives.description: AI advocates see PACMAN as a major step forward in experimental control: a machine can monitor, predict, and act thousands of times faster than a person. That speed is exactly what future fusion plants will need to prevent disruptions before they happen.

Critics worry about giving machine learning direct control of powerful experimental hardware. A model trained on past plasma behavior can fail when it encounters something new, so PACMAN still relies on exhaustive safety limits and human oversight before it could be trusted in a commercial power plant.

The article describes an engineering advance, not a physics discovery. PACMAN combines prediction, decision-making, and hardware safety in a modular way, making it easier to test and improve than a single black-box AI system.

If PACMAN works on more reactors and more types of instabilities, it could be scaled up to larger fusion machines and eventually to power-producing plants. Researchers will also need to prove that the AI stays reliable over long operating periods and under unusual plasma conditions.
